## Part B

Determining which ward has the most Starbucks per person and which wards have 0 Starbucks.

```{r, echo=FALSE}

```

```{r}

#joining the starbucks and the ward population data together
wards_starbs <- st_join(ottawa_strabs, ottawa_wards, join = st_within)

starbs_count <- as.data.frame(table(wards_starbs$name))
```

```{r}
#calculating the Starbucks in each ward

#getting the population data for each ward
ward_info <- merge(ward_pops, starbs_count, by = "Ward", all.x = TRUE)


#calculating the Starbucks per person in each ward
ward_info$starbs_per_person <- ward_info$n_starbucks/ward_info$pop

```


The Knowxdale-Merivale has the most wards per person with 0.00075 Starbucks per person.

# Question 2

```{r}
#downloading the elevation raster and the border of Zion national park
zion_elevation <- rast(system.file("raster/srtm.tif", package = "spDataLarge"))

zion_park_poly <- read_sf(system.file("vector/zion.gpkg", package = "spDataLarge"))

#transforming to WGS84 for OSM compatibility 
zion_park <- st_transform(zion_park_poly, 4326)

#extracting the bounding box for Zion National Park
zion_bbox <- st_bbox(zion_park)
bbox_vector <- c(zion_bbox["xmin"], zion_bbox["ymin"], zion_bbox["xmax"], zion_bbox["ymax"])
```

## Part A
Dowloading the hiking trails and plotting them on the evelation raster data.

I had to transform the Zion Park map to WGS84 (EPSG:4326) to ensure compatibility with OpenStreetMap (OSM) data. Initially, I was unable to query hiking trails from OSM because the map and the trail data were using different coordinate reference systems, which made spatial operations fail.

Additionally, the elevation raster data was provided in a UTM projection, so after retrieving and processing the trails in WGS84, I needed to transform everything into the UTM CRS to correctly overlay the vector and raster layers. Consistent CRS alignment was essential for accurate spatial analysis and visualization.

After a quick search on CHATGPT, I learnt that hiking trails are stored under the highway tag in OSM.  Therefore, the get this information about the hiking trails in Zion National Park, so the features with highway=path needed to be queried  to get all the information on walkable paths in the Zion National Park, since they are not labelled speicifcally as "hiking" trails in OSM.

```{r}
#dowloading the hiking trails from OSM
zion_hike_trails <- opq(bbox = bbox_vector) %>% 
  add_osm_feature(key = "highway", value = "path") %>% 
  osmdata_sf()
```


```{r}
#extracting the specific hiking trails as lines from OpenStreetMap
hike_trails <- zion_hike_trails$osm_lines

#making sure the trails are in the same CRS raster (UTM- not WGS84)
trails <- st_transform(hike_trails, crs(zion_elevation))
```

```{r}
#transforming the park boundary to the same CRS
zion_park_crs <- st_transform(zion_park_poly, crs(zion_elevation))

#converting to a vector so the raster could be cropped and masked to the shape of Zion National Park
zion_vector <- vect(zion_park_crs)

#cropping and masking raster
elev_crop <- crop(zion_elevation, zion_vector)
elev_mask <- mask(elev_crop, zion_vector)
```

```{r}
#clipping the trails to only stay in the boundary of Zion National Park
trails_clipped <- st_intersection(trails, zion_park_crs)

#converting the raster to a dataframe so it can be plotted with ggplot2
elev_df <- as.data.frame(elev_mask, xy = TRUE)
colnames(elev_df)[3] <- "elevation"

#making the plot
ggplot() +
  geom_raster(data = elev_df, aes(x = x, y = y, fill = elevation)) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "C") +
  geom_sf(data = trails_clipped, color = "green", size = 0.4) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "Hiking Trails in Zion National Park",
    fill = "Elevation (m)"
  ) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))


```


## Part B
Highlighting Angel's Landing Trail

```{r, include = FALSE}
#checking the names of the trails
names(trails)

#filtering to find Angel's Landing
angel_trail <- trails[grepl("angel", trails$name, ignore.case = TRUE), ]

#checking the trail pulled is close to what the actual Angel's Landing trail
plot(angel_trail$geometry)
```

From AllTrails, part of the West Rim Trail is combined with the Angles' Landing Trail to make the full Angels' Landing Hiking Trail.  Therefore, need to determine the where the trails meet up to determine where to cut the West Rim Trail.

```{r, include=FALSE}
west_rim_trail <- trails[grepl("west rim", trails$name, ignore.case = TRUE), ]
# Combine both layers and get bounding box
bbox <- st_bbox(rbind(west_rim_trail, angel_trail))


#making a visual of the west rim and the angels landing trail
plot(st_geometry(west_rim_trail),
     col = "blue",
     xlim = bbox[c("xmin", "xmax")],
     ylim = bbox[c("ymin", "ymax")],
     main = "West Rim & Angel's Landing Trails",
     xlab = "Longitude", ylab = "Latitude")

#adding Angel's Landing trail (red)
plot(st_geometry(angel_trail), col = "red", add = TRUE)


legend("bottomright", 
       legend = c("West Rim Trail", "Angel's Landing Trail"),
       col = c("blue", "red"),
       lty = 1, lwd = 2,
       bty = "n")

```
The above image indicates what line segments are going to be needed.  To get the full length of the trail as on https://www.alltrails.com/trail/us/utah/angels-landing-trail, I need to combine the red line with the blue line it intersects with to the south. OSM often breaks long trails into multiple segments which can be used to get the pieces of the West Rim Trail needed to make the full Angel's Landing Trail.

```{r, include=FALSE}
#checking the different line segments of the West Rim Trail
nrow(west_rim_trail)

# Check the IDs or names
unique(west_rim_trail$name)
unique(west_rim_trail$osm_id)  # if that column exists
```


```{r}
#making the full Angels Landing Trail using the ids of the different sections of the West Rim Trail

#excluding these segments based on the graph
exclude_ids <- c(14326789, 1215389944, 1014946428, 1014946429, 14326894)

#trimming the trail to exclude the unneeded ids
trim_west_rim <- west_rim_trail[!west_rim_trail$osm_id %in% exclude_ids,]

#combining all the line segments
full_angels_trail <- rbind(angel_trail, trim_west_rim)

#merginging into a single line string 
full_angels_trail <- st_union(full_angels_trail)
full_angels_trail <- st_cast(full_angels_trail, "LINESTRING")

#plot to confirm
plot(st_geometry(full_angels_trail))

```

## Part C
Determining the elevation gain of the trail

```{r}
# Force projection to UTM Zone 12N (units = meters)
angel_utm <- st_transform(full_angels_trail, crs = 32612)

angel_line <- st_cast(angel_utm, "LINESTRING")

#breaking the trail line segment into smaller segments 
trail_points <- st_line_sample(angel_line, density = 1/3)
trail_points <- st_cast(trail_points, "POINT")

#converting to sf object
trail_points <- st_sf(geometry = trail_points, crs = st_crs(angel_line))
```

```{r, results='hide'}
trail_vect <- terra::vect(trail_points)

#extracting the elevation 
elev_values <- terra::extract(zion_elevation, trail_vect)

#adding elevation to the points
trail_points$elevation <- elev_values[, 2]
```

```{r}
coords <- st_coordinates(trail_points)
distances <- sqrt(diff(coords[,1])^2 + diff(coords[,2])^2)
trail_points$distance <- c(0, cumsum(distances))
```

```{r}
ggplot(trail_points, aes(x = distance, y = elevation)) +
  geom_line(color = "darkgreen", size = 1) +
  labs(
    title = "Elevation Profile of Angel's Landing Trail",
    x = "Distance along trail (meters)",
    y = "Elevation (meters)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r}
# Compute elevation differences between consecutive points
elev_diff <- diff(trail_points$elevation)

# Keep only the positive (uphill) segments
elev_gain <- sum(elev_diff[elev_diff > 0])

# Print the total elevation gain
cat("Total elevation gain along the trail is", round(elev_gain), "meters\n")
```
he elevation gain profile I generated does not exactly match the graph provided by AllTrails, but it follows the same general trend. Specifically, there is a steady increase in elevation from the beginning of the trail, leading up to a peak around the 3.0 to 3.4 km mark, consistent with the AllTrails profile.

Some discrepancies may be due to additional trail length introduced during the stitching of trail segments, which could artificially increase both the total distance and cumulative elevation gain. Additionally, my elevation data was sampled at approximately every 3 meters, which may contribute to the more stepped or stair-like appearance of the graph, in contrast to the smoother incline shown on AllTrails.

Noticed the information I pulled from the GIS lab was incorrect because I had the same values for the Slope and Curvature, so I used the gis_bridge on Courselink to get better slope and curvature values.  I then replaced my columns I had previously with the corrected data.

```{r}
#pulling in the data from the bridge
#slope
slope_r <- rast("C:/Users/mckay/Downloads/slope.tif")
#plan curvature
c_plan_r <- rast("C:/Users/mckay/Downloads/plan_curvature.tif")
#profile curvature
c_prof_r <- rast("C:/Users/mckay/Downloads/profile_curvature.tif")

#converting the 'landslide_pred' data frame into a SpatVector of points
#using the 'x' and 'y' columns for geometry, and assigning the CRS of 'slope_r'
points <- vect(landslide_pred, geom = c("x", "y"), crs = crs(slope_r))

#combining the 3 raster layers into one raster stack then extracting the information
raster_stack <- c(slope_r, c_plan_r, c_prof_r)
extracted <- extract(raster_stack, points)

#replacing old Slope and Curvature
landslide_pred$Slope <- extracted[, 2]
#only using the plan curvature which give indication to flow direction
#ie- down like in landslides
landslide_pred$Curvature <- extracted[, 3]  
```

## Part B
Fitting models:

Model 1: with interactions (slope/curvature/elevation)

Model 2: without interactions

Setting up the tasks:
```{r}
landslide_pred[] <- lapply(landslide_pred, function(col) {
  if (is.character(col)) as.factor(col) else col
})

landslide_pred$Slope_Curv_Elev <- with(landslide_pred, Slope * Curvature * Z)

# # Model 2: Exclude elevation (Z), Slope, Curvature
baseline <- landslide_pred[, !names(landslide_pred) %in% c("Slope_Curv_Elev")]

#setting up the task for model 1- with interaction
task_mod1 = mlr3spatiotempcv::TaskClassifST$new(
                       id = "interaction_model",
                       backend = mlr3::as_data_backend(landslide_pred),
                       target = "lslpts",
                       positive = "TRUE", 
                       coordinate_names = c("x", "y"),
                       coords_as_features = FALSE, 
                       crs = "EPSG:32717")

#setting up task for model 2- without interaction- baseline model
task_mod2 = mlr3spatiotempcv::TaskClassifST$new(
                       id = "baseline",
                       backend = mlr3::as_data_backend(baseline),
                       target = "lslpts",
                       positive = "TRUE", 
                       coordinate_names = c("x", "y"),
                       coords_as_features = FALSE, 
                       crs = "EPSG:32717")
```

Setting up the Elastic-Net Learner:

```{r}
#defining the learner- Elastic Net logistic regression learner
learner_glmnet <- lrn("classif.glmnet", predict_type = "prob")

#2D search for best alpha and lambda
search_space <- ps(
  alpha = p_dbl(lower = 0, upper = 1),
  lambda = p_dbl(lower = 1e-4, upper = 1)
)

#adding 5 fold-cross validation 
cross_val <- rsmp("cv", folds = 5)

#grid search 
grid_search <- tnr("grid_search", resolution = 5)

#adding terminator 
terminator <- trm("evals", n_evals = 25)

#AutoTuner for Model 1 (with interaction)
auto_glmnet_mod1 <- AutoTuner$new(
  learner = learner_glmnet$clone(),  # clone so each gets its own learner
  resampling = cross_val,
  measure = msr("classif.auc"),
  search_space = search_space,
  tuner = grid_search,
  terminator = terminator
)

#AutoTuner for Model 2 (baseline)
auto_glmnet_mod2 <- AutoTuner$new(
  learner = learner_glmnet$clone(),
  resampling = cross_val,
  measure = msr("classif.auc"),
  search_space = search_space,
  tuner = grid_search,
  terminator = terminator
)

```

Training the model on both tasks 

```{r, results='hide'}
#training on all variables
auto_glmnet_mod1$train(task_mod1)
pred_mod1 <- (auto_glmnet_mod1$predict(task_mod1))

#training of baseline- no interaction
auto_glmnet_mod2$train(task_mod2)
pred_mod2 <- (auto_glmnet_mod2$predict(task_mod2))
```

## Part C
Comparing models

```{r}
#making the outer resampling 
outer_resample <- rsmp("spcv_coords", folds = 5)

#making the inner resampling 
inner_resample <- rsmp("cv", folds = 5)

#setting up the AutoTuner with the same process as above
terminator <- trm("evals", n_evals =25)
tuner <- tnr("grid_search", resolution =5)

search_space <- ps(
  alpha = p_dbl(lower = 0, upper =1),
  lambda = p_dbl(lower = 1e-4, upper =1)
)
  
  lerner_glmnet <- lrn("classif.glmnet", predict_type = "prob")
  
#creating the AutoTuner for each task
auto_mod1 <- AutoTuner$new(
  learner = learner_glmnet,
  resampling = inner_resample,
  measure = msr("classif.auc"),
  search_space = search_space,
  tuner = tuner,
  terminator = terminator, 
  id = "glmnet_mod1"
)

auto_mod2 <- AutoTuner$new(
  learner = learner_glmnet,
  resampling = inner_resample,
  measure = msr("classif.auc"),
  search_space = search_space,
  tuner = tuner,
  terminator = terminator,
  id = "glmnet_mod2"
)

```

```{r, results='hide'}
design <- rbind(
  benchmark_grid(task_mod1, auto_mod1, outer_resample),
  benchmark_grid(task_mod2, auto_mod2, outer_resample)
)

# Run the benchmark
bmr <- invisible(benchmark(design))

# Aggregate AUC results
auc_results <- invisible(bmr$aggregate(msr("classif.auc")))
```

```{r}
print(auc_results[, c("task_id", "learner_id", "classif.auc")])

```

##Part D
Plotting the distribution of the predicted probablities of the better model.

Model 2, without the interaction term, is the better model because the AUC for both those model using task 2 were higher.  A higher AUC, indicates the model is more accurate.

```{r}
# Predict using the better model
pred <- auto_glmnet_mod2$predict(task_mod2)

# Get the predicted probabilities and true labels
df_pred <- data.frame(
  prob = pred$prob[, "TRUE"],  # probability of landslide = TRUE
  truth = pred$truth
)

# Plot the distributions
ggplot(df_pred, aes(x = prob, fill = truth)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.6) +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Predicted Probabilities",
    x = "Predicted Probability of Landslide = TRUE",
    y = "Density",
    fill = "Actual Landslide"
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("TRUE" = "skyblue", "FALSE" = "red")) +
  theme_minimal()
```

The distribution graph was plotted using the baseline model, which did not include the interaction term between slope, curvature and elevation.  Therefore, this interaction term did not help with predicting landslides.  The graph itself looks reliable because the two classes are separated well on the graph.  The true curve is peaking closer to 1 and the false curve is peaking closer to zero.  However, there is still a sizable area that is overlapped between the two curves, which indicated where the model was unsure about whether a landslide occurred or not.

The baseline model outperformed the interaction model in terms of AUC. A likely reason is that the interaction term (Slope × Curvature × Elevation) introduced unnecessary complexity or noise into the model. This could have led to overfitting during training, reducing generalization performance when tested on new data. Additionally, the interaction may not have provided unique predictive information beyond what each variable already contributed individually.
